nameStory: The Carolina Grasshopper gets its name from the Carolina region where it was first scientifically described, though it actually ranges across most of North America. It's also called the "road-duster" because of its habit of kicking up little puffs of dust when it jumps from dirt roads and paths. Some folks call it the "quaker" due to the subtle rattling sound its wings make during flight.
description: The Carolina Grasshopper is a medium-sized hopper that's perfectly designed to disappear on dirt roads and gravelly paths. These short-horned grasshoppers range from about 1.25 to 2.25 inches long, with females being noticeably larger than males. Their bodies are typically grey to brown, helping them blend seamlessly with soil and gravel, but their real surprise comes when they take flight—flashing bold black wings bordered with bright yellow-white bands. You'll often mistake their fluttering flight pattern for a butterfly until they land and vanish again into the ground.

idTips.label: Black and yellow wing flash
idTips.description: When disturbed, watch for the dramatic flash of black wings with bright yellow-white borders during flight—this is your best field mark and completely unmistakable

idTips.label: Camouflaged body
idTips.description: At rest, the mottled grey-to-brown body matches dirt and gravel so perfectly you'll lose track of where it landed—run your eyes slowly over the ground to spot the still form

idTips.label: Road and path preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on or immediately next to dirt roads, gravel paths, and bare soil areas where they bask in the sun—rarely in thick grass

idTips.label: Butterfly-like flight
idTips.description: Flight pattern is fluttery and erratic like a large butterfly, not the strong, direct flight of many grasshoppers—often hovers briefly before landing

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Chunky, robust grasshopper about the length of your thumb (females) to pinky finger (males) with relatively short antennae for a grasshopper

habitat: Look for Carolina Grasshoppers along dirt roads, gravel paths, sandy areas, and other open, sunny spots with bare or sparsely vegetated ground throughout New England. They particularly favor disturbed areas like trail edges, parking areas, and roadside shoulders where the soil is compacted and vegetation is patchy. These sun-lovers avoid dense grasslands and shady areas, preferring the warm, dry conditions of open terrain.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but early individuals may be hard to spot as they're focused on feeding and are less likely to make dramatic flights.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible and active. Males perform hovering courtship flights over open ground, making this the best season for identification.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, continuing to be easily spotted until the first hard frosts. This is often when they're most numerous and easiest to observe.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frost. The species overwinters as eggs buried in the soil, so no grasshoppers are visible during winter months.

funFact: Carolina Grasshoppers are nature's ultimate magic trick—their camouflage is so perfect that researchers have found you can be staring directly at one on a dirt road and still not see it until it moves, even when you know exactly where to look.
confusionNotes: The fluttery flight often causes people to mistake Carolina Grasshoppers for butterflies until they land and disappear. Unlike true butterflies, they don't perch with wings held vertically and their wings fold straight back along the body when at rest. Other grasshoppers in the area lack the dramatic black and yellow wing flash.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the Carolina "Locust," this isn't a true locust like the biblical swarms—it's just an old-fashioned name for large grasshoppers. True locusts are a specific type of grasshopper that forms devastating swarms, while Carolina Grasshoppers are generally solitary and rarely cause crop damage.
compareHints: While there are no other Dissosteira species commonly found in New England, Carolina Grasshoppers can be distinguished from other band-winged grasshoppers by their specific black wings with yellow-white borders—other species might have red, orange, or clear wing bands. They're also more consistently found on bare ground and roads rather than in grassy areas where other band-winged species might be found.
